entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Georges de Selve was a French scholar, diplomat and ecclesiastic who played a pivotal role in the intellectual and religious landscape of 16th-century Western Europe.

Born into a prominent family, de Selve was educated at the University of Paris and later became a prominent figure in the French Renaissance humanist movement.

As a diplomat, de Selve served as a counselor to French monarchs Francis I and Henry II, and was involved in several key diplomatic missions, including the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1540.

De Selve was also a prolific writer and scholar, producing numerous works on theology, philosophy, and classical literature.

His most notable work, a four-volume commentary on the works of St. Augustine, showcased his erudition and intellectual depth, and remains an important source for scholars of Renaissance thought.

Despite his significant contributions to French diplomacy and scholarship, de Selve's life was cut short when he died on April 22, 1541, at the age of 60.

Georges de Selve's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as his writings and diplomatic efforts helped shape the intellectual and religious currents of 16th-century Europe.

The Treaty of Fontainebleau, which de Selve played a key role in negotiating, marked a significant turning point in the conflict between France and the Holy Roman Empire, and helped establish France as a major power in Western Europe.

Today, de Selve is remembered as a leading figure in the French Renaissance humanist movement, and his works continue to be studied by scholars of Renaissance thought and French history.
